commentary.headline: A small edit to one big file is xs's weak spot: xs-c++ takes longer to update the file than to copy it fresh
paragraphs: The clearest result today is a regression, not a win. We edited 4 KiB in the middle of a 4 GiB file. Rsync then beat both xs builds in every one of the ten matched cells across three runs. xs-c++ was worse. It ran at 0.43-0.46x rsync whenever the Mac or mars received, taking 11-13 s against rsync's 5 s. That is more than twice its own fresh copy of the same file (4.5-6.1 s). xs-rs ran at 0.67-0.83x. Each cell has 11-20 blocks, and the medians repeat across runs and builds. That makes this the most trustworthy finding of the day. It points at the delta-update path, not the network.

Fresh copies are still the big win: 2-3.5x rsync on the large file, the laikav2 project and the 1.35M-file csearchv3 tree. The two builds are usually within a few percent of each other. There are two exceptions, both specific to xs-rs and both measured over 17-20 blocks. First, pushing one big file from the Mac to mars, xs-rs managed only 1.45x (8.2 s against xs-c++'s 5.4 s), and a second run reproduced the gap. Second, on laikav2's 10% update xs-rs was slower than rsync in all three directions (0.85-0.89x), while xs-c++ won (1.17-1.24x).

No-op runs, where nothing has changed, favour xs-rs: 1.56-1.89x on laikav2, and 2.30x against xs-c++'s 1.80x on csearchv3, with less CPU than xs-c++. Yesterday's worker sweep used older builds and its run failed. It suggested 8 workers help a lot on a 711k-file no-op pull (14.3 s against 36.9 s with 4) but barely on a smaller tree. It also showed xs-c++ taking 104 s on that pull, slower than rsync. Treat all of these as leads. The csearchv3 cells have only 1-4 blocks.

reports.overview: These experiments provided useful tuning insights. Here are the insights: both xs versions copy new data two to three and a half times faster than rsync on every data set tried. Both lose to rsync when one small edit is made inside one very large file, and the C++ version is then slower than simply copying the file again. The Rust version is slightly slower than rsync on a mid-sized project after a 10% change, and noticeably slower than the C++ version when pushing one big file to mars. When nothing has changed, the Rust version checks fastest. More workers looked helpful on very large trees, but that comes from a failed run on older builds and is provisional.

commentary.headline: Eager writeback, not anchors or no-atomic, is what lets xs win durable local copies
paragraphs: The clearest result came from durable local copies of the 711,103-file psample corpus onto the T5 SSD. Eager writeback cut xs's median time to a durable copy from 223.6 s to 139.9 s. That is a 1.60x matched speedup across 12 blocks, and it also used about 38% less client CPU. This matters because plain xs loses this workload: in a separate run it was 0.90x of plain rsync. With eager writeback on both tools, xs was 1.29x faster than rsync over 6 blocks. That almost exactly matches the time ratio of 0.77 predicted from earlier screening. We can be reasonably confident for this disk, corpus and cold cache, but not beyond them.

Two hoped-for tweaks did nothing measurable locally. The larger parent-descriptor budget (the anchors arm) reached 0.88x of rsync on fresh copies, against 0.90x for plain xs. Adding no-atomic on top of eager writeback gained 1.3%, below the 5% target. A single, unpaired pull onto the Mac showed anchors halving no-op time. However, that run failed, and the Mac sentinel's xs-versus-xs check drifted by up to 17%, so this is a lead, not a finding.

Between neo and mars, xs's advantage depends heavily on workload and direction. No-op re-syncs and small-file trees show large wins, up to 7.8x on the deep small-file tree when neo receives. The 20,000-file mixed corpus sits near 0.9 Gb/s for every tool in both directions, which suggests a shared ceiling. The newest revision beat its parent in only one cell: deep-tree no-op into mars, 3.46 s versus 5.09 s. A single-block 2.09x psample no-op in the failed OS1b run points the same way. The neo-mars sentinel stayed within 4% on its self-checks, so these comparisons look stable.

reports.overview: These experiments provided useful tuning insights. Here are the insights: for full durable copies to the local SSD, turning on eager writeback made xs much faster, about 1.6 times its normal speed. With eager writeback on both tools, xs also beat rsync. Without it, xs was slightly slower than rsync. Re-syncing an unchanged backup was about twice as fast with xs. Two other tweaks, a larger descriptor budget and skipping atomic renames, did not help locally. Over the network, xs helps most for small-file trees and unchanged re-syncs, and not at all for the large mixed workload. These results are provisional and limited to the tested machines and data.

insights.title: Eager writeback is the big local durable-copy win
insights.finding: On fresh durable copies of psample to the T5 SSD, xs-eager was 1.60x faster than plain xs.
insights.evidence: 12 matched blocks: 139.85 s vs 223.60 s median. Throughput was 1.20 vs 0.75 Gb/s. Client CPU was 140.8 vs 226.7 s.
insights.caveat: Covers one corpus, one cold-cache local SSD target and one revision. Medians only, with no significance test.

insights.title: Eager writeback flips xs versus rsync on fresh local copies
insights.finding: With eager writeback on both tools, xs was 1.29x faster than rsync, matching the predicted time ratio of about 0.77. Without it, plain xs was 0.90x of plain rsync.
insights.evidence: Eager run, 6 blocks: 139.0 s vs 181.0 s, with client CPU of 131.5 vs 193.6 s. Plain run, 6 blocks: xs 230.0 s vs rsync 209.5 s.
insights.caveat: The two runs use different revisions and times, so this is not a controlled comparison. Rsync-eager at 181.0 s versus plain rsync at 209.5 s hints that eager writeback helps rsync too. That is a hypothesis.

insights.title: Anchors and no-atomic show no local benefit; Mac anchors result unverified
insights.finding: The larger parent-descriptor budget did not beat plain xs locally. No-atomic added only 1.3% over eager writeback. One Mac no-op pull showed anchors twice as fast as xs.
insights.evidence: LC12 fresh: anchors 0.88x vs xs 0.90x of rsync (236.7 s vs 230.0 s). LC12 no-op: 1.96x vs 1.98x. LC11, 4 blocks: 1.013x, with CPU 125.1 vs 132.7 s. MA8: 27.3 s vs 55.9 s, 1 sample each, unpaired.
insights.caveat: MA8 failed, has no rsync arm and no matched blocks. The Mac sentinel's xs-versus-xs check drifted beyond 5% in 4 of 8 cells.

insights.title: neo-mars: big gains on small trees and no-ops, a flat ceiling on mixed data
insights.finding: Xs's edge over rsync depends strongly on corpus and direction. The mixed-bimodal fresh copy runs at about 0.88 to 0.90 Gb/s for every tool in both directions.
insights.evidence: OS1a, 4 blocks each: small-deep no-op 7.83x into neo (rsync 16.98 s) but 1.00x into mars. Small-flat fresh 1.38x into mars vs 1.00x into neo. Small-flat no-op 2.72x and 3.18x. Mixed fresh 0.99x both ways. E1n single blocks agree (3.21x, 1.36x, 1.00x).
insights.caveat: The flat mixed-corpus rate across tools suggests a link or host bottleneck. This is a hypothesis; S3 shows xs at 7.2 Gb/s for the same corpus on the separate 10 GbE link.

insights.title: New revision beats its parent only on no-ops into mars
insights.finding: The newest revision and its parent tie within about 4% in 11 of 12 OS1a cells. The exception is small-deep no-op into mars, where the parent trails badly.
insights.evidence: OS1a, 4 blocks: xs 3.46 s (1.00x rsync) vs parent 5.09 s (0.70x). OS1b, 1 block: psample no-op into mars, xs 15.0 s vs parent 31.4 s (2.09x), rsync 33.6 s.
insights.caveat: OS1b failed with single samples, and its reverse direction is unpaired. The data does not label which host runs which operating system.

insights.title: CPU cost of xs depends on which side runs it
insights.finding: As the sending client, xs uses roughly 2 to 4x rsync's client CPU. As the receiving client on deep trees, and in eager local copies, it uses less.
insights.evidence: OS1a sender: mixed fresh 10.98 vs 5.38 s. Small-deep fresh 10.11 vs 4.85 s. Small-deep no-op 4.30 vs 1.18 s. OS1a receiver: small-deep fresh 18.36 vs 26.85 s, small-deep no-op 5.30 vs 9.38 s.
insights.caveat: Only client CPU is reported, not the remote side. These are medians over 4 to 6 blocks.

insights.title: neo-mars sentinel stable; Mac-mars sentinel noisy
insights.finding: On neo-mars, xs-versus-xs ratios stayed within 0.96 to 1.02. On Mac-mars, 4 of 8 cells fell outside the 5% band.
insights.evidence: S4 also shows rsync 1.064x of xs on small-flat fresh into neo, versus 0.72x the other way. S3 xs-versus-xs values: 0.833 (mixed fresh into Mac), 1.080, 1.063, 0.944.
insights.caveat: Each cell has only 2 blocks. S3 ran on the parent revision and uses wall time, not time-to-durable.

limitations: Medians over 1 to 12 matched blocks, with no confidence intervals or significance tests.
OS1b and MA8 failed, and E1n is still running with single blocks per cell.
Cross-run comparisons mix revisions, dates, timing metrics (wall vs durable) and cache states.
Mac-link measurements showed xs-versus-xs drift above 5%, weakening Mac-side conclusions.
Host operating systems are not labelled in the data, so receiver-OS effects cannot be attributed.

commentary.headline: Eager writeback, not worker count, is what moves a local psample backup; the Mac pull stays stuck on scanning
paragraphs: The most useful result of the day came from the local Pi-to-T5 series. Without any flush setting, xs cannot beat rsync on a cold first copy of psample: it ran at 0.91 to 0.96 of rsync across LC1, LC3 and LC6, and every tool, cp and a single tar stream included, landed in a 210 to 265 second band around 0.75 Gb/s, which reads as a drive-bound ceiling rather than a tool difference. The one thing that broke the band was eager writeback: xs-eager reached a durable copy in 140 s against 224 s for plain xs (1.58x, 4 matched blocks) and 182 s for rsync-eager, and the follow-up head-to-head now running shows 1.29x over rsync-eager on 3 blocks, close to the 0.77 time ratio the screening predicted. The same arm also used about 40 percent less client CPU. That is a strong lead, though the arm's flag is not in the supplied metadata and the run is incomplete.

Worker count turned out to be a CPU lever, not a time lever: two workers matched the default four within 0.2 percent while spending 24 percent less CPU, one and sixteen workers were about 18 percent slower, and the source-guard build gave no time gain, exactly as the development log expected. On the no-op resync, by contrast, xs was 1.93x faster than rsync locally, yet the identical corpus pulled onto the Mac still runs at 0.67 of rsync with seven times rsync's CPU, and none of MA7's five variants moved it by more than 4 percent. Together with rsync's 1.81x win on the small-deep no-op into the Mac, the pattern points at directory handling on APFS rather than transfer speed, which is what the parent-directory budget change targets; nothing in this window tests that change yet.

On the 10 GbE link the picture is otherwise comfortable: the receiver-defaults build was never more than 2 percent slower and 9 to 20 percent faster in small no-op and single-file cells over 12 blocks, and the shape confirmation holds xs at 1.7 to 4.1x rsync on compressible trees and large text, delivering 8 to 8.8 Gb/s on large text. The hourly sentinel, however, shows A/A ratios of 0.77 to 1.13 with only two blocks per cell, so small effects on the Mac need more blocks than that.

development.summary: Three engine changes were logged: capping receiving workers at four with a faster peer check, skipping source-path resolution on local copies, and a larger budget of retained parent directories to stop walking destination paths from the root. The first was confirmed on the Mac link in this window, the second showed no time gain here, and the third was motivated by this window's Mac pull but is not yet tested in it. Two lab fixes addressed a voided local block and a bad run-time estimate.

reports.overview: These experiments provided useful tuning insights. Here are the insights: on the Pi's local backup to the USB drive, eager writeback is the one setting that clearly shortens the time until the copy is safely on disk, and it also saves CPU; this is provisional until the running head-to-head finishes. Changing the worker count does not speed the local copy, but two workers do the same work with noticeably less CPU. Re-syncing an unchanged tree locally is almost twice as fast with xs as with rsync. Pulling the same tree onto the Mac remains slower than rsync and no tested setting fixes it; the cause looks like directory handling, which a pending code change targets. The capped-receiver build is safe to keep on the Mac link.

insights.title: Eager writeback cuts local durable time by a third and saves CPU
insights.finding: On the cold psample copy to the T5, xs-eager reached durability in 140.0 s versus 223.7 s for plain xs (1.58x) and 182.0 s for rsync-eager; the running head-to-head puts xs-eager at 1.29x rsync-eager (140.7 vs 180.7 s).
insights.evidence: LC3: 4 paired blocks per arm; client CPU 140.9 s (xs-eager) vs 229.9 s (xs). LC9: 3 paired blocks, CPU 133.5 vs 193.3 s.
insights.caveat: LC9 is still running with 3 blocks; the eager arm's setting is not in the supplied tuning flags, so the mechanism is inferred from the arm name only. Single USB SSD, cold cache, one corpus.

insights.title: Without eager flush every tool hits the same local ceiling; xs trails rsync slightly
insights.finding: Cold fresh psample: rsync 212.4 s, xs 231.5 s (0.91x), cp-r 241.5, cp-a 246.1, tar 265.4 (0.80x). LC6 and LC3 repeat xs at 0.96x and 0.94x of rsync. All arms deliver 0.63 to 0.80 Gb/s.
insights.evidence: LC1 4 blocks; LC6 4 blocks (xs 221.6 vs rsync 210.0 s); LC3 4 blocks (223.7 vs 213.0 s).
insights.caveat: The hypothesis that xs would approach a tar stream is overturned: tar is the slowest. A drive-write bound is a hypothesis, not measured. The earlier LC1 attempt was stopped with 3 invalid samples.

insights.title: Worker count is a CPU knob, not a time knob, on the four-core Pi
insights.finding: -j2 matched the default (221.5 vs 226.4 s, 1.002x) with 173 vs 227 s CPU; -j1 0.81x, -j16 0.82x, -j8 0.95x, with CPU rising to 311 s at 16. In LC6, -j2/-j3 and the source-guard builds all sat at 0.90 to 0.95x rsync.
insights.evidence: LC2: 4 paired blocks per arm. LC6: 4 blocks; guard-j2 224.7 s vs j2 229.5 s, guard-j3 232.9 vs j3 220.7 s.
insights.caveat: Differences of a few percent between 4-block medians are within the spread seen elsewhere; the source-guard result confirms the log's by-hand finding of no time gain.

insights.title: Same corpus, opposite result: local no-op resync favours xs, the Mac pull favours rsync
insights.finding: Locally with cold caches xs re-synced unchanged psample in 65.7 s vs rsync's 126.5 s (1.93x, lower CPU 56 vs 78 s). Pulled onto the Mac, xs took 54.2 s vs rsync 37.0 s (rsync 1.49x) with 196 vs 28 s client CPU; at 1% update 59.1 vs 44.3 s.
insights.evidence: LC4: 6 paired blocks. MA7: 6 paired blocks (no-op), 4 to 6 (update).
insights.caveat: Different machines, cache states and primary metrics (durable_s vs wall_s); this is an interaction across runs, not a controlled comparison. The log attributes the Mac cost to per-directory path walking; that is a hypothesis the data here cannot test.

insights.title: None of MA7's receiver settings recovers the Mac pull; eight workers doubles CPU for nothing
insights.finding: xs-O, --no-atomic, eight receiver workers and four scanners all landed at 0.99 to 1.04x of plain xs on both scenarios; recv8 raised client CPU to 358 to 360 s from about 200 s.
insights.evidence: MA7: 90 samples, 18 invalid; no-op cells 6 paired blocks each, update cells 2 to 6 paired blocks.
insights.caveat: 18 invalid samples and uneven pairing in the update cell weaken the 1% figures. Only --no-atomic has a supplied flag; the other variants' settings are not in the metadata.

insights.title: Capped receiver workers: faster in several cells, slower nowhere meaningful
insights.finding: xs-recv4 vs parent: 1.13x small-flat no-op push, 1.10x mixed-bimodal no-op push, 1.09x mixed-bimodal no-op pull, 1.09 to 1.20x on the single-file cells, 1.04x small-deep fresh pull; lowest ratio 0.98x (mixed-bimodal fresh pull).
insights.evidence: E6b: 720 of 720 samples valid, 12 paired blocks in every cell.
insights.caveat: The gains are concentrated in sub-second cells where the Mac's noise is largest in relative terms; the recv4 setting has no supplied flag.

insights.title: xs's weak spot on the Mac link is deep trees received on APFS, not bytes
insights.finding: rsync beat xs 1.81x on the small-deep no-op pull (5.37 vs 9.61 s, xs CPU 33.5 vs 4.7 s), while xs was 4.45x faster pushing the same tree. On compressible corpora xs holds 1.73 to 4.12x over rsync, with large-text at 8.0 to 8.8 Gb/s on 10 GbE and less CPU than rsync (9.5 vs 21.5 s).
insights.evidence: E6b small-deep cells 12 blocks; MA6 confirm 12 blocks per cell; MA6 screening 2 to 3 blocks agrees.
insights.caveat: Linking the small-deep and psample deficits to directory handling is a hypothesis across runs with different corpora; the push/pull asymmetry also differs in which host does the metadata work.

insights.title: The hourly sentinel is noisier than its 5% target at two blocks
insights.finding: A/A ratios ranged from 0.77 (mixed-bimodal no-op push, s0003) and 0.82 (small-flat no-op push, s0002) to 1.13 (mixed-bimodal fresh pull, s0003). rsync's small-flat fresh push swung from 5.0 s (s0001) to 17.1 s (s0003) against a steady 3.6 to 3.9 s for xs.
insights.evidence: Four sentinel runs, 48 valid samples each, 2 paired blocks per cell.
insights.caveat: Two blocks cannot separate drift from noise; the xs-to-rsync direction never flipped, so there is no sign of a regression, only of variance.

limitations: All figures are window-only medians over 2 to 12 matched blocks with no confidence intervals or significance tests.
Local runs use a single corpus, one USB SSD and cold caches with durable_s; Mac/mars runs use wall_s and warm caches, so cross-link ratios are not comparable.
LC9 is incomplete (3 blocks); MA7 has 18 invalid samples and uneven pairing; the first LC1 attempt was voided.
Several arm settings (eager, recv4, recv8, scan4, xs-O) have no supplied tuning flags, so their mechanisms are inferred from names only.
Throughput for no-op cells divides corpus bytes by wall time and is not a wire rate.
nextSteps: Let LC9 complete and, if the eager advantage holds, run eager arms on the no-op and 1% update local scenarios.
Pair -j2 against the default on the Pi with more blocks and record CPU as a secondary metric.
Run the planned MA8/LC12 paired blocks for the parent-directory budget build against its parent on the psample pull and local copies.
Raise the sentinel's blocks per cell or widen its tolerance before treating A/A deviations as drift.
Add a deep-tree no-op pull cell to any receiver-side change so the small-deep gap is tracked.

commentary.headline: Eager writeback, not workers, is the local lever; the Mac-as-receiver gap survives every tweak
paragraphs: The most useful surprise came from the Pi-to-T5 backup. Every tool, including a single tar stream, lands within 0.63 to 0.80 Gb/s on the cold first copy, and plain rsync is actually the fastest at about 210 s while xs sits at 0.90 to 0.96 times that across five variants. Changing worker counts, adding the source-guard fix, or dropping the temp-file rename moves nothing. The one thing that does is eager writeback: xs-eager reached a durable copy in 140 s against 224 s for default xs and 182 s for rsync-eager, with 4 matched blocks, and the new head-to-head run is tracking the same gap on its first block. The practical reading is that this path is flush-bound, so the win is in overlapping flushing with copying, not in parallelism. Confidence is moderate: four blocks, one corpus, one drive.

On the 10 GbE Mac/mars link the picture is split by direction. With the Mac sending, xs is 2.4 to 4.1 times faster than rsync on compressible trees and large text files, confirmed over 12 blocks. With the Mac receiving, xs loses on psample (rsync 1.34 to 1.49 times faster) and on the deep small-file no-op (rsync 1.81 times), while burning six to seven times rsync's CPU. None of the five receiver tweaks tried recovered any of it, and eight receiver workers doubled CPU for a 4 percent change. That failure is itself informative: the cost is probably not in the knobs we exposed.

The sentinel runs also tell us how much to trust small cells: same-tool repeats drift up to 25 percent on sub-second no-ops with two blocks, and rsync's time in one cell swung from 5 to 17 s. Cells under a second should not drive decisions without many more blocks.

reports.overview: These experiments provided useful tuning insights. Here are the insights: On the Pi backup to the external SSD, turning on eager writeback got the copy safely written about a third sooner, and that was the only change that helped; more or fewer workers, skipping the rename, and the source-guard fix made no difference, and rsync remains marginally fastest by default. Re-syncing an unchanged local backup is about twice as fast with xs. Over the fast Mac link, xs is two to four times faster than rsync when the Mac sends, but slower and far more CPU-hungry when the Mac receives, and none of the receiver tweaks fixed that. Capping receiver workers at four is safe. These are provisional findings from small numbers of repeats.

insights.title: Eager writeback is the only local win
insights.finding: On the cold first copy of psample to the T5, xs-eager reached a durable copy in 140.0 s versus 223.7 s for default xs (1.58×) and 182.0 s for rsync-eager (1.23× over xs), while client CPU fell from 229.9 to 140.9 s. The running eager-vs-eager follow-up shows xs-eager 137.4 s against rsync-eager 179.3 s.
insights.evidence: LC3: 4 paired blocks per arm; LC9: 1 paired block for xs-eager, 2 for rsync-eager.
insights.caveat: Metric is time to durable copy, so eager writeback mostly moves flushing earlier rather than reducing work; LC9 is incomplete. Mechanism is a hypothesis.

insights.title: Local cold copy is tool-insensitive and rsync leads by default
insights.finding: All tools deliver 0.63–0.80 Gb/s: rsync 212.4 s, xs 231.5 s (0.91×), cp-r 241.5 s, cp-a 246.1 s, single tar stream 265.4 s. In LC6, five xs variants (default, -j2, -j3, with and without the source-guard fix) landed at 0.90–0.96× rsync's 210.0 s.
insights.evidence: LC1: 4 paired blocks per arm; LC6: 4 paired blocks per arm.
insights.caveat: Hypothesis: the USB SSD write/flush path is the ceiling, so tool choice cannot matter much here. One corpus, one drive; an earlier LC1 attempt had 3 invalid samples.

insights.title: Worker count: 2 matches 4 at lower CPU; 1, 8 and 16 are slower
insights.finding: xs-j2 221.5 s (1.00× default 226.4 s) with 173 vs 227 CPU-s; xs-j8 0.95×, xs-j1 0.81×, xs-j16 0.82× with 311 CPU-s.
insights.evidence: LC2: 4 paired blocks per arm.
insights.caveat: Four-core Pi writing to one USB drive; differences of a few percent are within what this block count can resolve.

insights.title: Local unchanged re-sync: xs nearly twice as fast as rsync
insights.finding: With cold caches, a no-op re-sync of psample took xs 65.7 s and rsync 126.5 s (1.93×), with less client CPU (56.4 vs 78.4 s).
insights.evidence: LC4: 6 paired blocks.
insights.caveat: Only the no-op cell appears in this window; the 1% change scenario named in the question has no samples here.

insights.title: Mac as receiver stays slower than rsync and no tweak helps
insights.finding: Pulling psample onto APFS: rsync 37.0 s vs xs 54.2 s at no-op (rsync 1.49×) and 44.3 vs 59.1 s after a 1% update (1.34×). Skipping directory times, no-atomic, four scanners and eight receiver workers all stayed within 0.99–1.04× of xs; recv8 doubled client CPU to ~360 s. xs client CPU was 197–202 s vs rsync 28–32 s. E6b shows the same pattern on small-deep no-op into the Mac: rsync 5.37 s vs xs 9.61 s (1.81×).
insights.evidence: MA7: 4–6 paired blocks per cell, 18 of 90 samples invalid; E6b: 12 blocks.
insights.caveat: Unequal block counts across MA7 arms; what the Mac receiver spends its CPU on is not measured here.

insights.title: Mac as sender and compressible data: xs 2.4–4.1× rsync, confirmed
insights.finding: Fresh real-congress mac→mars 6.67 vs 27.49 s (4.12×); large-text mac→mars 7.79 vs 19.13 s (2.47×, 8.8 vs 3.6 Gb/s); large-text mars→mac 2.90×; real-congress mars→mac 1.73×. The screening run gave 3.76, 2.40, 3.04 and 1.64×. Strong direction asymmetry: real-congress fresh takes 6.7 s out of the Mac but 46.2 s into it.
insights.evidence: MA6-confirm: 12 paired blocks per cell; MA6 screening: 4.
insights.caveat: Why compressible corpora favour xs (compression, streams or both) is not separable from these arms.

insights.title: Capping receiver workers at four is safe
insights.finding: xs-recv4 vs parent across 20 cells ranged 0.98–1.20×; gains of 9–20% appeared only in sub-second or tiny cells (tiny-one, mixed-bimodal and small-flat no-ops). The two slower cells were 0.982 and 0.987×.
insights.evidence: E6b: 12 paired blocks per cell, 720 samples, 0 invalid.
insights.caveat: The gains sit in cells where sentinel A/A noise is of the same size, so treat them as 'no harm' rather than wins.

insights.title: Sentinel: short cells are noisy, rsync especially
insights.finding: Same-tool repeats ran 0.77–1.13× on sub-second no-ops (e.g. mixed-bimodal mac→mars 0.767×, small-flat mac→mars 0.825×), breaking the 5% stability hypothesis there. rsync in small-flat fresh mac→mars took 5.03, 10.45, 17.06 and 9.41 s across the four runs, so the xs/rsync ratio swung 0.22–0.78.
insights.evidence: S3 s0001–s0004: 2 paired blocks per cell, 48 samples each.
insights.caveat: Two blocks per cell; whether rsync's variance is host load or tool behaviour is unknown.

limitations: All figures are window-only medians over 1–12 matched blocks with no confidence intervals; differences under ~5% are not resolvable in most cells.
LC9 is still running with one xs-eager block; MA7 has 18 invalid samples and unequal block counts; the first LC1 attempt was stopped with 3 invalid samples.
Local results come from one corpus, one Pi and one USB SSD; Mac results from one APFS receiver.
Eager-writeback arms carry no recorded tuning flags, so the exact configuration cannot be stated from this data.
Experiments with different arms are not controlled comparisons of each other; cross-run patterns are observations, not tests.
nextSteps: Let LC9 finish to at least 4–6 paired blocks before treating xs-eager as the local backup candidate.
Profile the Mac receiver (CPU breakdown) rather than adding more receiver knobs.
Run the missing 1% update scenario for LC4.
Increase sentinel blocks on sub-second cells or drop them from the drift check.

reports.overview: These experiments provided useful tuning insights. Here are the insights: when the backup on the external drive was already up to date and nothing was cached, the new tool finished about twice as fast as rsync and used less processor time. This held in every one of six matched rounds. The planned test after 1% of files change has no results yet. For a fresh full copy, the two tools were about equal. Eager writeback looked promising for both tools, and most so for the new tool. Skipping the temp-file rename did not help. Each fresh-copy result comes from a single run, so those findings are provisional leads, not settled defaults.

insights.title: xs roughly halves no-op re-sync time versus rsync on a cold cache
insights.finding: On a cold-cache no-op re-sync of the psample backup (711,103 files, about 21.0 GB) onto the local SSD, xs had a median durable time of 65.7 s. rsync took 126.5 s. The median paired speed was 1.93x rsync across 6 matched blocks.
insights.evidence: xs: 6 valid samples, 6 paired blocks, median 65.71 s, paired speed 1.926x. rsync: 6 valid samples, median 126.54 s. Corpus bytes divided by durable time come to 2.56 versus 1.33 Gb/s. No invalid samples.
insights.caveat: These are medians from 6 blocks on one host, one SSD and one corpus, with no significance test. The Gb/s figure is corpus size divided by time. It is not the volume of data actually moved in a no-op.

insights.title: xs also used less client CPU on the no-op re-sync
insights.finding: Median client CPU was 56.4 s for xs and 78.4 s for rsync, about 28% less for xs, alongside the faster completion.
insights.evidence: medianClientCpuSeconds: xs 56.381, rsync 78.4355, each from 6 blocks.
insights.caveat: Only client-side CPU was reported. Total system CPU, including kernel and filesystem work, may differ.

insights.title: The 1% change scenario is missing from the evidence
insights.finding: The re-sync experiment asked about both a no-op and a 1% file change. Only the no-op cell appears in this window, so the 1% change claim remains untested here.
insights.evidence: LC4 run state is complete with 12 samples, all in the noop cell (6 per arm). There is no cell for the change scenario.
insights.caveat: The change scenario may have run outside this six-hour window or not at all. That cannot be determined from the supplied data.

insights.title: Fresh full copy: default xs and default rsync are at parity
insights.finding: For a fresh cold copy of psample, default xs and default rsync finished in nearly the same durable time. The roughly 2x advantage xs showed on the no-op re-sync did not appear on the fresh copy.
insights.evidence: xs 216.4 s and rsync 215.1 s. rsync paired speed was 1.006x versus xs, from 1 block each.
insights.caveat: Single block per arm. This contrast spans two different experiments and scenarios, so it is an observation, not a controlled comparison. One hypothesis is that the fresh copy is limited by write and flush work on the SSD rather than by tool overhead.

insights.title: Eager writeback shortened time-to-durable for both tools, most for xs
insights.finding: The xs-eager arm reached durability in 139.2 s, 1.55x faster than default xs. The rsync-eager arm took 182.0 s, 1.19x faster than default xs and about 15% faster than default rsync.
insights.evidence: xs-eager 139.17 s, paired 1.555x. rsync-eager 181.97 s, paired 1.189x. Control xs 216.38 s. Each value is from 1 block.
insights.caveat: One block per arm makes this a promising lead only. The eager arms list no tuningFlags, so the exact mechanism and settings are not specified in the evidence.

insights.title: Skipping the temp-file rename did not help and looked slightly worse
insights.finding: xs with --no-atomic took 234.7 s, 0.92x the speed of default xs. That was the slowest arm in the fresh-copy run.
insights.evidence: xs-noatomic 234.74 s, paired 0.922x, client CPU 234.4 s, from 1 block.
insights.caveat: Single block, so the roughly 8% slowdown could be run-to-run noise. Whatever the direction, the evidence does not support giving up the temp-file rename for speed.

insights.title: In the fresh-copy run, client CPU closely tracked wall time
insights.finding: In the fresh-copy run, each arm's client CPU seconds were close to its durable seconds. Arms that finished sooner also consumed less client CPU. The eager arms therefore showed no visible CPU penalty.
insights.evidence: CPU versus durable time: xs 216.6 vs 216.4 s, xs-eager 140.9 vs 139.2 s, xs-noatomic 234.4 vs 234.7 s, rsync 229.1 vs 215.1 s, rsync-eager 194.7 vs 182.0 s.
insights.caveat: 1 block each. Why CPU matches wall time so closely is unexplained. It may reflect how CPU is measured or time spent in kernel flush work. This is a hypothesis to check, not a finding.

limitations: The fresh-copy durability experiment has only 1 valid block per arm, so its rankings are screening-level only.
The 1% change scenario for re-sync is absent from this window.
All results come from one host, one local SSD target, one corpus and a cold cache. Network links, warm caches, other storage and other directions were not tested.
Ratios are window medians of matched blocks, with no confidence intervals or significance testing.
Eager-writeback arms list no tuningFlags, so their exact settings cannot be stated from the evidence.
Throughput figures are corpus bytes divided by durable time, not wire or disk rates. This matters most for no-op runs, where little data actually moves.
Comparisons across the two experiments involve different scenarios and arm sets and are not controlled.
nextSteps: Run the 1% change re-sync scenario with matched xs and rsync blocks on the same cold-cache setup.
Repeat the fresh-copy durability experiment with at least 5 to 6 blocks per arm to confirm the eager-writeback gains, especially xs-eager.
Document the exact settings behind the eager arms so a confirmed result can be reproduced.
Re-test --no-atomic with more blocks before drawing a direction, and weigh any gain against crash-safety implications.
Add warm-cache runs, and a network or remote case, to see whether the no-op re-sync advantage holds beyond a cold local SSD.
Record system and kernel CPU alongside client CPU to explain why CPU tracks wall time in fresh copies.

tuningImplications.recommendation: Prefer xs over rsync -aH for cold-cache no-op re-syncs of this backup on the local SSD. Treat this as a well-supported candidate for this workload, not a general default. Do not extend the claim to partial-change re-syncs until that scenario is measured.
tuningImplications.tradeoffs: xs was faster (65.7 s vs 126.5 s) and used less client CPU (56.4 s vs 78.4 s), so no CPU penalty was observed. The evidence covers only one corpus, one local SSD, a cold cache and a no-op change set.
tuningImplications.evidenceStrength: Moderate for the no-op cold-cache local case: 6 matched blocks, consistent median 1.93x, no invalid samples. No evidence for the 1% change case.
tuningImplications.nextTest: Run the 1% change scenario with at least 6 matched blocks per arm on the same setup, then repeat with a warm cache.

tuningImplications.recommendation: Treat eager writeback as a promising lead for shortening time-to-durable on fresh local copies, most of all with xs. Keep the temp-file rename, because --no-atomic showed no benefit. Do not adopt any setting from this run without replication.

reports.overview: These experiments provided useful tuning insights. Here are the insights: when copying the psample backup to the local USB SSD, turning on eager writeback in xs was the only change that clearly sped up the time until data is safely on disk. It was about 1.6 times faster than plain xs and also faster than rsync, but this comes from only three paired runs in an unfinished experiment, so it is a provisional candidate. Changing the number of workers did not help. The default of four was about as fast as two. Two workers used noticeably less processor time. Without eager writeback, xs was slightly slower than rsync in every setup tried. The source-guard fix did not change speed in a consistent way.

insights.title: Eager writeback in xs is the standout provisional win
insights.finding: Observation: in the durability experiment, xs-eager reached durable completion in a median of 140.8 s. Plain xs took 227.7 s. That is a median paired speed of 1.60x control over 3 matched blocks. Delivered throughput was 1.20 Gb/s versus 0.74 Gb/s. It was also the only arm in any run to exceed about 0.92 Gb/s.
insights.evidence: LC3 cell real-psample fresh, neo to neo-ssd, cold cache. xs-eager: 140.811 s, 1.1957 Gb/s, paired speed 1.599, 3 blocks. xs control: 227.681 s, 0.7395 Gb/s, 3 blocks.
insights.caveat: The run is still in progress, and each arm has only 3 matched blocks. These are medians, not significance tests. The labels do not say what eager writeback does mechanically, and it has no supplied tuning flag.

insights.title: Eager writeback also helps rsync, but less
insights.finding: Observation: rsync-eager had a median of 182.9 s and 1.29x the xs control over 2 blocks. Plain rsync had 212.8 s and 1.09x over 3 blocks. That is roughly a 14 percent shorter median durable time for rsync. For xs the reduction was about 38 percent. Hypothesis: durable time is dominated by post-copy flushing, and eager writeback overlaps that flushing with the copy. xs may benefit more because of how it schedules writes.
insights.evidence: LC3: rsync-eager 182.936 s, paired 1.290, 2 blocks. rsync 212.769 s, paired 1.094, 3 blocks. xs-eager 140.811 s versus xs 227.681 s.
insights.caveat: rsync-eager was not paired directly against plain rsync. The comparison between the two rsync arms uses medians from different block counts (2 versus 3), and the mechanism is unverified.

insights.title: Skipping the temp-file rename gives a modest, uncertain gain
insights.finding: Observation: xs with --no-atomic had a median of 209.1 s, which is 1.13x the xs control over 2 blocks. This is far smaller than the eager writeback gain. It also removes the atomic temp-file-then-rename behaviour, which is a durability and consistency tradeoff.
insights.evidence: LC3 xs-noatomic: 209.063 s, 0.806 Gb/s, paired 1.131, 2 blocks.
insights.caveat: Only 2 blocks, in an incomplete run. Combining it with eager writeback was not tested.

insights.title: Without eager writeback, xs did not beat rsync
insights.finding: Observation: in the dedicated head-to-head, every xs arm was slower than rsync. Paired speeds ranged from 0.902 to 0.958 over 4 blocks each. rsync had a median of 210.0 s. Default xs was closest at 221.6 s and 0.958x. The durability run agrees: plain rsync was 1.09x the xs control. The hypothesis that xs with two or three workers matches rsync is not supported here.
insights.evidence: LC6, 4 blocks per arm, 0 invalid. xs 0.958, xs-j3 0.948, xs-guard-j2 0.935, xs-j2 0.923, xs-guard-j3 0.902, all relative to rsync at 210.004 s. LC3 rsync was 1.094x xs.
insights.caveat: These are medians from 4 blocks. The gaps of 4 to 10 percent are small enough that more blocks are needed before calling them firm.

insights.title: Worker count: four and two are equivalent; one, eight and sixteen are slower
insights.finding: Observation: in the worker sweep, -j2 matched the default at 232.4 s versus 232.3 s, a paired speed of 0.9996. -j1 was 0.826x, -j8 0.881x and -j16 0.760x. In the head-to-head, -j2 and -j3 were slightly slower than default xs, at 229.5 s and 220.7 s versus 221.6 s. Hypothesis: one USB SSD sets a ceiling around 0.72 to 0.80 Gb/s for non-eager durable copies, so extra workers mostly add contention.
insights.caveat: The sweep has only 1 block per arm, so its ordering is fragile. The head-to-head only compared xs arms against rsync, not against each other directly.

insights.title: Fewer workers cut processor time at little speed cost
insights.finding: Observation: client CPU seconds scaled with worker count. In the sweep, CPU was 138 s at one worker, 186 s at two, 235 s at the default four, 279 s at eight and 341 s at sixteen. In the head-to-head, -j2 used 177 s and guard -j2 used 170 s, versus 228 s for default xs and 228 s for rsync. That is roughly 22 to 26 percent less CPU, for about 1 to 4 percent longer durable time. Eager xs used only 141 s of CPU while also being fastest, which is a surprise.
insights.evidence: LC2 medianClientCpuSeconds: 138.1, 185.6, 235.1, 279.4, 341.1. LC6: xs-j2 177.3, xs-guard-j2 169.5, xs 228.5, rsync 228.0. LC3: xs-eager 140.9 versus xs 236.0.
insights.caveat: CPU figures are medians from small samples. The reason eager writeback lowers CPU is unknown and could reflect how CPU time is attributed during flushing.

insights.title: The source-guard fix shows no consistent speed effect

insights.title: Baselines were stable across runs

limitations: All evidence comes from one workload: the psample corpus, a fresh copy, local copy to a USB SSD, and cold cache. It says nothing about network transfers, warm cache, incremental updates or other storage.
The durability experiment is still running. Several arms have only 2 matched blocks.

tuningImplications.recommendation: Treat xs with eager writeback as the leading provisional candidate for getting psample durably onto the local SSD sooner. Do not adopt it as a default until the running experiment completes with more blocks. Skipping the atomic rename gives a much smaller gain and weakens durability semantics, so do not prioritise it.

tuningImplications.evidenceStrength: Weak to moderate. There were 3 matched blocks for xs-eager and 2 for xs-noatomic and rsync-eager, in an incomplete run.
tuningImplications.nextTest: Complete the run with at least 5 matched blocks per arm, adding a paired comparison of xs-eager against rsync and rsync-eager.

tuningImplications.recommendation: Without eager writeback, xs at two or three workers, with or without the guard fix, did not match rsync on this workload. Keep rsync as the speed reference for plain copies. Consider -j2 only as a CPU-saving option, not a speed improvement.
tuningImplications.tradeoffs: All xs arms ran at 0.90 to 0.96x rsync speed. -j2 cut client CPU to about 170 to 177 s, versus about 228 s for default xs and rsync.
tuningImplications.evidenceStrength: Moderate for the negative result, with 4 matched blocks per arm. The guard comparison is confounded by the two code revisions.
tuningImplications.nextTest: Compare xs with eager writeback against rsync with paired blocks. Re-test the guard fix on a single revision.

tuningImplications.evidenceStrength: Weak. Each arm has a single block.

evidenceRuns.question: With four cores and one USB drive, does xs copy psample to the T5 faster with 1, 2, 8 or 16 workers than with its default 4?
evidenceRuns.hypothesis: On a four-core Pi writing to one USB SSD, a worker count other than the default four copies psample faster.

evidenceRuns.question: Between the Mac and mars at 10 GbE, has anything drifted? Does xs still match itself, and xs against rsync stay put?
evidenceRuns.hypothesis: Hour by hour, the A/A ratio stays within 5% of 1 and the xs to rsync ratio stays where E6b's rsync arm put it.

evidenceRuns.question: On a first backup of psample from the Pi's NVMe to a Samsung T5, with nothing cached, how much faster is xs -aH than rsync -aH, cp -a and cp -r, and how close does any tool come to one tar stream?
evidenceRuns.hypothesis: Copying psample locally from NVMe to the T5 with cold caches, xs -aH is faster than rsync -aH and cp -a, and near a single tar stream.

evidenceRuns.question: Does capping the receiver at four workers, and reaping the peer sooner, make xs faster than its parent anywhere and slower nowhere, between the Mac and mars?
evidenceRuns.hypothesis: xs with at most four receiving workers and a backed-off peer wait is faster than its parent in at least one cell into mars and slower in none, both ways.

reports.overview: These experiments provided useful tuning insights. Here are the insights: on the Pi copying to one USB SSD, the default four workers and two workers were about equally fast, and two used noticeably less CPU. One or sixteen workers were slower. In that local copy, rsync beat xs and the other tools, so xs has no local advantage yet. Between the Mac and mars, the version that caps receiving workers at four was usually a little faster, especially for single tiny files, but was slightly slower in three cases. Repeat runs of the same xs version varied by up to about 18 percent, so the small gains are provisional. xs was much slower than rsync on one no-change check of many small, deeply nested files sent to the Mac.

insights.title: Pi to USB SSD: two and four workers tie, and two uses less CPU
insights.finding: Both ends of the worker range hurt. Two workers matched the default four. One worker and sixteen workers were slower. Throughput stayed near 0.76 Gb/s whatever the worker count, which looks like a ceiling.
insights.evidence: The default (4 workers) took 220.5 s at 0.764 Gb/s using 226 CPU-s. Speed relative to the default, from matched blocks: 2 workers 1.004 (3 blocks, 219.0 s, 173 CPU-s); 8 workers 1.009 (3 blocks, 228.5 s median, 264 CPU-s); 1 worker 0.787 (3 blocks, 278.9 s, 135 CPU-s); 16 workers 0.921 (2 blocks, 264.2 s, 302 CPU-s).
insights.caveat: The run is still in progress, with only 2 to 3 blocks per worker count. The 8-worker arm has a paired ratio above 1 but a slower median time, so it is effectively a tie. The idea that the USB SSD is the bottleneck is a hypothesis; it was not measured.

insights.title: Local first backup: rsync was fastest and the single tar stream slowest
insights.finding: The hypothesis that xs beats rsync locally was not supported in this window. The single tar stream, meant as a reference point, was the slowest tool rather than an upper bound.
insights.evidence: Speed relative to rsync, 4 matched blocks each: xs 0.910 (231.5 s compared with 212.4 s), cp-r 0.877, cp-a 0.863, tar 0.799 (265.4 s). CPU: rsync 228.5 s, xs 240.8 s, cp about 118 to 122 s, tar 195.5 s.
insights.caveat: Only 4 blocks. This is one corpus on one SSD with cold caches. The xs time here (231.5 s) differs from the xs default in the worker run (220.5 s), but those runs were not controlled against each other.

insights.title: Capping receivers at four: faster in 17 of 20 cells, slower in 3
insights.finding: The receiver-cap variant was faster than its parent in most cells. Its largest gains were on single tiny files. It was 2 to 3 percent slower in three larger fresh or real-data cells, so the 'slower nowhere' hypothesis is not strictly met.
insights.evidence: Single tiny file: speed 1.117 to 1.232 (6 blocks each), for example 0.237 s to 0.193 s. Real-congress fresh, mars to Mac: 1.044 (85.6 s to 71.6 s). Small-deep fresh, Mac to mars: 1.130. Below 1: mixed-bimodal fresh, mars to Mac, 0.969; real-congress no-change, mars to Mac, 0.985; real-congress fresh, Mac to mars, 0.977. In mixed-bimodal fresh, Mac to mars, the paired ratio is 1.005 but the median time was worse (1.815 s compared with 1.646 s).
insights.caveat: There were 6 to 7 blocks per cell, and the run spans two code revisions. Most effects are under 10 percent, which is within the repeat-run variation seen in the sentinel. That the tiny-file gain comes from reaping the peer sooner is a hypothesis.

insights.title: Regression: rsync is 1.86 times faster than xs on the small-deep no-change check sent to the Mac
insights.finding: In one cell rsync clearly beat xs, and xs used far more CPU there.
insights.evidence: Small-deep, no-change run, mars to Mac: xs took 10.67 s using 37.9 CPU-s. rsync took 5.53 s using 5.0 CPU-s. rsync's speed relative to xs was 1.857 (6 blocks). The receiver-cap variant barely helped (1.027, 10.39 s). In the opposite direction (Mac to mars) xs took 3.24 s and rsync was 0.213 times xs speed.
insights.caveat: This is one corpus and one direction. The cause is not measured; per-directory overhead on the Mac receiver is a hypothesis.

insights.title: Strong direction asymmetry: fresh copies into the Mac are much slower
insights.finding: With the same corpus, fresh transfers from mars to the Mac took several times longer than fresh transfers from the Mac to mars.
insights.evidence: xs fresh: real-congress 85.6 s mars to Mac compared with 8.5 s Mac to mars. Small-deep 51.3 s compared with 7.8 s. Small-flat 19.3 s compared with 3.85 s. rsync shows the same pattern (92.8 s compared with 41.5 s on real-congress).
insights.caveat: Direction is confounded with which machine acts as client and with each machine's storage. The data cannot say whether the Mac's filesystem or the receiver code is responsible.

insights.title: xs beats rsync widely between the Mac and mars
insights.finding: Except for the small-deep no-change cell into the Mac and the single tiny file, xs was faster than rsync. The gap was largest for fresh copies to mars.
insights.evidence: Fresh copies, Mac to mars, rsync speed relative to xs: real-congress 0.203, small-deep 0.256, mixed-bimodal 0.339, small-flat 0.473. Real-congress no-change, Mac to mars: 0.263. Single tiny file: rsync 0.857 to 1.103.
insights.caveat: 6 to 7 blocks per cell, all with warm caches. The no-change mixed-bimodal cells report 29 to 47 Gb/s, above the 10 GbE link speed, because almost no data moves; they reflect metadata speed, not wire speed.

insights.title: Sentinel: repeat runs of xs drift up to about 18 percent; the xs-to-rsync ratios are broadly stable
insights.finding: Only 4 of 8 same-version comparisons stayed within 5 percent, which breaks the sentinel's stability hypothesis for this window. The xs-to-rsync ratios landed close to the values in the receiver-cap experiment.
insights.evidence: Repeat run relative to xs: 0.825 (small-flat no-change, Mac to mars), 0.938, 1.051 and 1.109 fall outside 5 percent; 0.972, 0.985, 1.001 and 1.018 fall inside. rsync relative to xs, sentinel compared with receiver-cap experiment: mixed-bimodal fresh, mars to Mac, 0.446 compared with 0.451; small-flat no-change, mars to Mac, 0.574 compared with 0.656; small-flat no-change, Mac to mars, 0.496 compared with 0.430.
insights.caveat: Only 2 blocks per cell. The largest deviations are in runs under one second, where small timing jitter matters most.

insights.title: Receiver cap trims CPU on heavy receiving work
insights.finding: Where the Mac was the receiving client on heavy fresh copies, the cap lowered CPU use while also lowering time.
insights.evidence: Small-deep fresh, mars to Mac: 109.7 CPU-s to 96.6 CPU-s. Real-congress fresh, mars to Mac: 95.3 CPU-s to 81.5 CPU-s. In most other cells CPU was within a few percent.
insights.caveat: CPU was measured on the client only. CPU use on mars was not measured in the Mac-to-mars direction.

limitations: These are medians over 2 to 7 matched blocks. There are no confidence intervals or significance tests.
The worker-count run on the Pi is still running, and the 16-worker arm has only 2 blocks.
The repeat-run variation in the sentinel (0.825 to 1.109) is larger than most of the receiver-cap effects.
The receiver-cap experiment spans two code revisions.
Direction, client role and storage are confounded between the Mac and mars.
No-change throughput figures exceed the link speed and reflect metadata work, not network rate.
Local results cover one corpus, one SSD and cold cache only.
nextSteps: Finish the Pi worker run, then compare two and four workers head to head with more blocks, recording CPU and durable completion time.
Profile xs on small-deep no-change runs into the Mac to explain why it is 1.86 times slower than rsync and uses about 7.6 times more CPU.
Rerun the receiver cap only on cells longer than about 5 seconds, plus tiny-file cells, with more blocks on a single revision.
Investigate why rsync beats xs on local cold copies to the USB SSD, for example by checking how much time goes to the final flush to disk.
Increase sentinel blocks per cell, or lengthen the shortest cells, to bring repeat-run noise down below the size of the effects being tested.

tuningImplications.recommendation: Avoid one worker and sixteen workers on this four-core Pi writing to a USB SSD. Two workers is a provisional candidate: it was as fast as the default four and used less CPU. Do not change the default until the run completes.
tuningImplications.tradeoffs: Two workers took 173 CPU-s compared with 226 CPU-s for the default, at about the same speed (1.004). Eight and sixteen workers add CPU (264 and 302 CPU-s) with no gain.
tuningImplications.evidenceStrength: Weak. The run is incomplete, with 2 to 3 blocks per worker count.
tuningImplications.nextTest: Complete the run, then do a paired comparison of the default against two workers with at least 8 blocks on the same storage, cold cache.

tuningImplications.recommendation: For local cold first backups to the USB SSD, rsync remains the fastest measured option. xs offers no local speed advantage yet (0.910 times rsync). Do not use the single tar stream as a speed ceiling.
tuningImplications.tradeoffs: cp used about half the CPU of rsync and xs but was 12 to 14 percent slower. xs used slightly more CPU than rsync.
tuningImplications.evidenceStrength: Moderate for this single setup (4 blocks per tool). It does not generalise beyond this storage and corpus.
tuningImplications.nextTest: Repeat on the code revision with the best worker setting from the worker-count run, and record where the time goes in the durable flush.

tuningImplications.recommendation: The receiver cap is a promising candidate (17 of 20 cells faster, with clear gains on tiny files), but it is not proven slower nowhere. Three cells were 2 to 3 percent slower. Keep it under evaluation, not as a default.
tuningImplications.tradeoffs: It lowers receiver CPU on heavy fresh copies into the Mac. It may slightly slow large fresh real-data and mixed-size copies.
tuningImplications.evidenceStrength: Moderate. 6 to 7 blocks per cell, but most effects are within the sentinel's repeat-run noise, and the run spans two revisions.
tuningImplications.nextTest: Run a single-revision comparison focused on the three regressed cells and the tiny-file cells, with more blocks. Separately, investigate the small-deep no-change regression against rsync into the Mac.

tuningImplications.recommendation: Treat differences under about 10 to 18 percent in sub-second cells as indistinguishable from noise. The xs-to-rsync ratios look stable, but the repeat-run stability goal was not met in half the cells.
tuningImplications.tradeoffs: None for tuning. This experiment defines the noise floor for interpreting other results.
tuningImplications.evidenceStrength: Weak. Only 2 blocks per cell.
tuningImplications.nextTest: Add blocks or lengthen the very short cells, and track the repeat-run ratio hour by hour.

reports.overview: These experiments provided useful tuning insights. Here are the insights: between the Mac and mars, xs was consistently faster than rsync on first copies. It was about 2.5 to 4 times faster when the Mac sends and about 1.5 to 3 times faster when mars sends. Large files moved at about 8 to 9 gigabits per second, close to the 10 gigabit link. One clear exception stood out: re-checking an already-synced deep tree of small files from mars to the Mac, rsync was faster. Capping receive workers at four looks provisionally neutral to slightly helpful, but its gains are similar in size to run-to-run noise. The local Pi backup test has produced no usable data yet.

insights.title: xs beats rsync on first copies, most strongly when the Mac sends
insights.finding: Observation: on fresh copies, xs beat rsync in every Mac-to-mars cell by large margins, and by smaller margins from mars to the Mac.
insights.evidence: Real-congress fresh, Mac to mars: xs 4.12x rsync (12 matched blocks, 6.67 s vs 27.49 s). The earlier screen showed 3.76x (4 blocks). Mars to Mac: 1.73x (12 blocks, 46.19 s vs 78.04 s) and 1.64x (4 blocks). Real-psample: 3.05x Mac to mars (2 blocks, 76.2 s vs 220.8 s) and 1.45x mars to Mac (1 matched block).
insights.caveat: Direction is confounded with which machine acts as client, and with each machine's storage. The psample result rests on 1 to 2 blocks. These are medians, not significance tests.

insights.title: Large files approach the 10 GbE ceiling with xs, using less CPU
insights.finding: Observation: on 8 large text files (8.6 GB), xs delivered roughly 8 to 9 Gb/s, against roughly 2.8 to 3.6 Gb/s for rsync. Client CPU was also less than half of rsync's.
insights.evidence: Mac to mars: xs 2.47x (12 blocks), 8.82 vs 3.59 Gb/s, client CPU 9.5 s vs 21.5 s. Mars to Mac: 2.90x (12 blocks), 8.00 vs 2.76 Gb/s, CPU 10.3 s vs 25.8 s. The screen run agreed, at 2.40x and 3.04x (4 blocks each).
insights.caveat: Throughput is corpus bytes divided by wall time. Hypothesis: xs is now near the link limit for large files, so further tuning there may yield little.

insights.title: Regression: rsync wins the deep small-file no-op check from mars to Mac
insights.finding: Observation: on the already-synced small-deep tree with mars sending, rsync was faster than xs and used far less client CPU. The same corpus in the opposite direction strongly favoured xs.
insights.evidence: Small-deep no-op, mars to Mac: rsync 1.77x xs (6 blocks), 5.25 s vs 9.24 s, client CPU 4.7 s vs 33.0 s. Mac to mars: rsync 0.23x xs (5 blocks), 11.09 s vs 2.60 s. Small-deep fresh, mars to Mac: xs only about 1.13x rsync (rsync 0.889, 5 blocks).
insights.caveat: Hypothesis only: the cost may come from directory walking or comparison on the receiving client in deep trees. This is not isolated, because client role and direction change together.

insights.title: Capping receivers at four workers: small gains, mostly in fast cells
insights.finding: Observation: the four-worker receiver variant was faster than its parent in 13 of 20 cells. Its largest gains came in sub-second or tiny cells. It was 0.6 to 2.1 percent slower in six cells.
insights.evidence: Small-flat no-op Mac to mars 1.19x (6 blocks). Mixed-bimodal no-op 1.13x and 1.10x. Tiny-one 1.07 to 1.22x. Fresh mixed-bimodal 1.03 to 1.05x. Slower cells: small-deep fresh mars to Mac 0.979 (5 blocks), small-deep no-op mars to Mac 0.985, small-flat 0.987 and 0.991, real-congress no-op Mac to mars 0.994.
insights.caveat: The sentinel's identical-arm ratios ranged from 0.91 to 1.08. Most of these differences are therefore within plausible noise. The hypothesis of being slower nowhere is not cleanly met. The run is still running and spans two code revisions.

insights.title: Sentinel shows run-to-run noise above 5 percent
insights.finding: Observation: xs compared against itself fell outside the 5 percent band in four of eight cells.
insights.evidence: Identical-arm ratios were 0.912 (mixed fresh, mars to Mac), 0.930 (small-flat no-op, Mac to mars), 1.066 and 1.079. The other four fell between 0.98 and 1.03. Each cell has 2 blocks.
insights.caveat: With 2 blocks per cell this may reflect sample size rather than drift. It still sets a practical floor for interpreting gains of 10 percent or less.

insights.title: Surprise: rsync much faster in the sentinel on small-flat fresh Mac to mars
insights.finding: Observation: most sentinel xs-versus-rsync ratios matched the earlier run closely, but one cell diverged sharply.
insights.evidence: Small-flat fresh Mac to mars: rsync took 5.03 s in the sentinel (ratio 0.78, 2 blocks) versus 13.08 s in the earlier run (0.29, 5 blocks). Mixed fresh Mac to mars was 0.27 vs 0.39. Other cells agreed within a few points, for example mixed no-op mars to Mac at 0.845 vs 0.845.
insights.caveat: Cause unknown. It could be timing, cache state or sample size. It deserves a check before treating rsync as stable.

insights.title: Client CPU tradeoff depends on workload
insights.finding: Observation: xs used more client CPU than rsync on no-op checks, but similar or less on fresh large copies.
insights.evidence: Real-congress no-op mars to Mac: 11.6 s vs 4.0 s. Small-flat no-op Mac to mars: 0.70 s vs 0.32 s. Real-congress fresh mars to Mac: 58.8 s vs 93.5 s. Psample: 178.5 s vs 187.5 s (Mac to mars) and 604 s vs 639 s (mars to Mac).
insights.caveat: Only client-side CPU was measured. Server-side cost is unknown.

insights.title: Local Pi backup comparison produced no valid data
insights.finding: Observation: both samples in the local NVMe-to-T5 comparison were invalid, so no cells exist.
insights.evidence: 2 samples, 2 invalid, 0 cells. The run is still running.
insights.caveat: No claim about xs, cp or tar locally can be made yet.

reports.overview: These experiments provided useful tuning insights. Here are the insights: on this Mac-to-Mars link with a large tree of about 711,000 files, the new tool (xs) copied fresh data about four times faster than rsync when the Mac sent, and about 1.4 times faster when the Mac received, using similar client CPU. For re-syncs, xs was much faster when the Mac sent, both when nothing changed and after a 1% update. It was slower than rsync for a 1% update pulled onto the Mac, and it used far more CPU there. The receive-to-Mac path is the weak spot. The incremental results rest on only two rounds each, so they are provisional. The fresh-copy confirmation is still running.

insights.title: Fresh copy, Mac sending: xs about 4x faster at lower CPU
insights.finding: On a fresh copy of the 711,103-file, 21.0 GB tree, xs beat rsync by a wide margin when the Mac sent to Mars. It also used slightly less client CPU.
insights.evidence: Median paired speed was 4.04x control over 10 matched blocks. Median wall time was 54.98 s for xs versus 218.90 s for rsync, equal to 3.06 versus 0.77 Gb/s of corpus bytes over wall time. Median client CPU was 174.2 s for xs versus 188.7 s for rsync.
insights.caveat: The run is still in progress. These are window medians with no confidence intervals. The corpus, link and warm-cache state are a single combination.

insights.title: Fresh copy, Mac receiving: xs wins but by much less
insights.finding: When Mars sent to the Mac, xs was still faster than rsync, clearing the hypothesis threshold of more than 5% faster. The margin was far smaller than in the other direction, and client CPU was essentially the same for both tools.
insights.evidence: Median paired speed was 1.43x over 10 matched blocks. Median wall time was 263.66 s for xs versus 368.54 s for rsync, equal to 0.64 versus 0.46 Gb/s. Median client CPU was 594.9 s for xs versus 589.2 s for rsync.
insights.caveat: Direction and client role change together: the client is the sender in one direction and the receiver in the other. The direction effect cannot be separated from client placement. The run is incomplete.

insights.title: Strong direction asymmetry: receiving on the Mac is the bottleneck
insights.finding: Both tools were much slower, and the client used much more CPU, when the Mac was the receiver. The effect was larger for xs.
insights.evidence: xs took 263.66 s receiving versus 54.98 s sending, about 4.8x longer. rsync took 368.54 s versus 218.90 s, about 1.7x longer. The client was the Mac in both cells, and its median CPU rose from 174.2 s to 594.9 s for xs and from 188.7 s to 589.2 s for rsync, with 10 blocks each.
insights.caveat: This is an observation across different cells, not a controlled comparison. One hypothesis is that file creation or metadata cost on the Mac receiving side dominates, but nothing here measures storage or filesystem behaviour directly.

insights.title: Re-sync with Mac sending: xs fast for both no-op and 1% update
insights.finding: With the Mac as sender, xs re-synced about 3.4x to 4x faster than rsync. Its time barely changed between a no-op and a 1% update.
insights.evidence: For the no-op, xs took 24.40 s versus 82.48 s for rsync, a paired speed of 3.39x over 2 blocks. For the 1% update, xs took 24.22 s versus 96.93 s, a paired speed of 3.99x over 2 blocks. Median client CPU was about 107 s for xs versus 67.0 s (no-op) and 74.1 s (update) for rsync.
insights.caveat: Only 2 blocks per cell. The Gb/s figures of up to 6.97 are total corpus bytes divided by wall time, not data actually moved, so they should not be read as wire throughput. xs used roughly 1.4 to 1.6x more client CPU here.

insights.title: Regression: 1% update pulled onto the Mac is slower with xs
insights.finding: For a 1% update with Mars sending to the Mac, xs was slower than rsync and used far more client CPU.
insights.evidence: Median paired speed was 0.82x over 2 matched blocks. Median wall time was 59.55 s for xs versus 48.65 s for rsync. Median client CPU was 204.5 s for xs versus 37.5 s for rsync, about 5.4x more.
insights.caveat: Only 2 blocks, so this is provisional. It matches the fresh-copy pattern of the Mac receiving side being expensive for xs, but that link is a hypothesis.

insights.title: Surprise: rsync incremental is faster when the Mac receives
insights.finding: rsync's 1% update was about twice as fast when Mars sent to the Mac as when the Mac sent to Mars. This reverses the fresh-copy direction pattern, and xs did not show the same benefit.
insights.evidence: rsync 1% update took 48.65 s with Mars sending versus 96.93 s with the Mac sending, 2 blocks each. xs took 59.55 s versus 24.22 s for the same two cells.
insights.caveat: The two cells differ in direction and in client placement (receiver versus sender). This is an uncontrolled cross-cell observation, and the cause is unknown.

insights.title: Coverage gap in the incremental question
insights.finding: The incremental experiment asks about a no-op each way, but no no-op cell with Mars sending to the Mac appears in this window. Fresh-copy evidence is also limited to the warm-cache state.
insights.evidence: MA4 reports 12 samples across 3 cells: no-op mac to mars, 1% update mac to mars, and 1% update mars to mac. All 3 cells use a warm cache.
insights.caveat: The missing cell may exist outside this six-hour window. Its absence here is not evidence of failure.

reports.overview: These experiments provided useful tuning insights. Here are the insights: when the Mac sends to mars, the new tool (xs) was clearly faster than rsync. It was about four times faster for a first full copy, a re-check with nothing changed, and a re-sync after a small change. When mars sends to the Mac, xs still won a first full copy by a smaller margin. It was slower than rsync for re-syncs, and its CPU use there was far higher. Copies into the Mac were slow for both tools and for two different senders. These are early results from only two to four repeats per case, so xs is a direction-specific candidate, not a proven default. The compression comparison on the neo link produced no usable data.

insights.title: xs is a strong win for fresh copies from Mac to mars
insights.finding: In the completed bidirectional run, xs copied the 711,103-file, about 21 GB psample tree from Mac to mars at a median 3.94x the speed of rsync. It also used less client CPU.
insights.evidence: Across 4 matched blocks, median wall time was 88.6 s for xs versus 288.8 s for rsync. Median delivered rate was 1.94 Gb/s versus 0.58 Gb/s. Median client CPU was 185.6 s versus 233.3 s.
insights.caveat: Medians from 4 blocks with no significance testing. The cache was warm, the client was the sender, and there was a single tree and link.

insights.title: Fresh copies into the Mac are slow for both tools, and xs gains less there
insights.finding: From mars to Mac, xs was still faster at a median 1.42x, but both tools were roughly 4 to 5 times slower than xs going the other way.
insights.evidence: Across 4 matched blocks, median wall time was 381.4 s for xs versus 456.6 s for rsync, or 0.45 versus 0.37 Gb/s. Client CPU was 712.3 s for xs versus 661.0 s for rsync. For comparison, xs took 88.6 s from Mac to mars.
insights.caveat: Direction is confounded with client role. The client is the sender when going to mars and the receiver when going to the Mac, and the hosts differ. The cause of the asymmetry is not identified.

insights.title: xs re-syncs from Mac to mars are about 3.5 to 4x faster than rsync, at a CPU cost
insights.finding: For warm re-syncs from Mac to mars, xs beat rsync both when nothing had changed and after 1% of files changed. However, it used more client CPU.
insights.evidence: No-op: xs at 4.04x rsync over 2 matched blocks, 29.1 s versus 121.0 s, with client CPU 122.5 s versus 90.2 s. After a 1% update: xs at 3.50x over 2 matched blocks, 28.3 s versus 97.5 s, with client CPU 121.3 s versus 75.6 s.
insights.caveat: Only 2 blocks per cell, and the run is still in progress. The Gb/s figures for these cells are corpus size divided by wall time, not actual data moved.

insights.title: Regression: xs re-syncs from mars to Mac are slower than rsync and much more CPU-hungry
insights.finding: With mars sending and the Mac as the receiving client, xs lost to rsync for both re-sync scenarios. It used roughly 6 to 7 times more client CPU.
insights.evidence: No-op: xs at 0.62x rsync over 3 matched blocks, 61.2 s versus 38.0 s, with client CPU 213.2 s versus 29.9 s. After a 1% update: xs at 0.72x over 2 matched blocks, 59.5 s versus 43.0 s, with client CPU 211.1 s versus 35.2 s.
insights.caveat: Small samples in a running experiment. Direction, client role and host are confounded. The high CPU is an observation; its cause, for example receiver-side scanning or hashing, is only a hypothesis.

insights.title: Surprise: rsync re-syncs are much faster in the mars to Mac direction
insights.finding: rsync completed warm re-syncs about 2.3 to 3.2 times faster from mars to Mac than from Mac to mars. This is the opposite of the fresh-copy asymmetry.
insights.evidence: rsync no-op took 38.0 s from mars to Mac (3 blocks) versus 121.0 s from Mac to mars (2 blocks). rsync after a 1% update took 43.0 s versus 97.5 s (2 blocks each).
insights.caveat: This compares cells with a different direction and client role, so it is not a controlled comparison. It suggests the file-tree scan cost depends on which host does the scanning, but that is a hypothesis.

insights.title: xs re-sync time looks fixed by scanning the tree, not by how much data changed
insights.finding: xs no-op and 1% update times were nearly identical within each direction. This points to a floor set by walking about 711k files rather than by moving data.
insights.evidence: From Mac to mars, xs took 29.1 s for a no-op versus 28.3 s after a 1% update. From mars to Mac, it took 61.2 s versus 59.5 s.
insights.caveat: The interpretation that tree scanning is the bottleneck is a hypothesis. Only 2 to 3 blocks per cell, and the update being slightly faster than the no-op is within plausible noise.

insights.title: Throughput is far below the 10 GbE link for fresh copies of many small files
insights.finding: The best fresh-copy rate observed was 1.94 Gb/s (xs, Mac to mars). Copies into the Mac stayed at or below 0.45 Gb/s on both the mars and neo links.
insights.evidence: From the bidirectional run: 1.94 and 0.58 Gb/s from Mac to mars, and 0.45 and 0.37 Gb/s from mars to Mac. From the stopped neo run, neo to Mac: 0.42 Gb/s for xs versus 0.34 Gb/s for rsync, in 1 block.
insights.caveat: The rates are corpus bytes divided by wall time. Seeing slow copies into the Mac from two different senders suggests a bottleneck on the Mac side, such as writing files or creating metadata, but this is untested.

insights.title: The Mac/neo experiment gave almost no usable evidence, and compression is untested
insights.finding: One neo run failed with its single sample invalid. The other was stopped after one matched block, which covered only neo to Mac and only the uncompressed rsync and xs arms.
insights.evidence: In that one block, xs ran at 1.25x rsync: 396.6 s versus 495.2 s, with client CPU 690.8 s versus 734.8 s. The compressed arms (rsync-z and xs-z) have no samples in this window.
insights.caveat: A single block is anecdotal. Nothing can be said about compression or the Mac to neo direction.

limitations: All results are medians from 1 to 4 matched blocks per cell, with no confidence intervals or significance tests.
The incremental experiment is still running, and the neo experiment produced one failed run and one stopped run.
Direction is confounded with client role (the client is the sender in one direction and the receiver in the other) and with host hardware and storage.
Only one tree (psample, 711,103 files, about 21 GB) was tested, and only with a warm cache. Cold-cache and other workloads are untested.
No tuning flags were supplied for any arm, so no worker, stream or other parameter effects can be assessed.
The compression arms produced no data.
Gb/s figures for re-sync scenarios reflect corpus size divided by wall time, not bytes actually transferred.
nextSteps: Finish the incremental run and add blocks so each re-sync cell has at least 4 to 5 matched blocks.
Separate direction from client role by running mars to Mac with the client on the sender side, and vice versa.
Profile xs client CPU during mars to Mac re-syncs to test whether receiver-side scanning or hashing explains the 6 to 7x CPU gap.
Investigate the slow copies into the Mac (about 0.37 to 0.45 Gb/s across two senders) with local write and file-creation baselines on the Mac.
Rerun the Mac/neo experiment after diagnosing the invalid sample, covering both directions and the compressed arms.
Add a cold-cache variant before generalizing any fresh-copy result.
