reports.overview: These experiments provided useful tuning insights. Here are the insights: on the local network, the tuned xs setting with four receiver workers and non-atomic writes repeatedly sped up fresh copies of many small files by roughly 1.3 to 1.7 times. It did not help on larger or real-world trees, and it trades away atomic file replacement. For no-change re-syncs it helped some trees and slightly hurt one. xs beat rsync in most incremental and fresh-copy cases, with a notable exception at 10% changed files on a large-file tree. Compression cost no time on data that does not compress. All of this is provisional and comes from small samples on a few machine pairs.

insights.title: Tuned setting reliably speeds small-file fresh copies, not larger trees
insights.finding: Observation: the tuned xs arm (4 receiver workers, --no-atomic) was faster than plain xs -z on fresh small-flat copies from neo to freya in all 9 replicate runs. On real-congress and mixed-bimodal it hovered around parity.
insights.evidence: Small-flat neo to freya: medians 1.28 to 1.66x across 8 complete runs (3 matched blocks each) and 1.59x in the stopped run (1 block). Example: 2.08 s vs 3.48 s. Real-congress: 0.94 to 1.08x. Mixed-bimodal: 0.89 to 1.04x. Client CPU on small-flat was similar or lower (about 4.5 to 5.4 s vs 4.9 to 7.2 s).
insights.caveat: The two changes, workers and non-atomic writes, were applied together, so their separate effects are unknown. Only 3 blocks per run.

insights.title: xs -z stays well ahead of rsync -z forward, but direction matters
insights.finding: Observation: from neo to freya, rsync -z took about 2.3 to 3.6 times as long as xs -z on small-flat and real-congress, and about 1.4 to 1.6 times as long on mixed-bimodal. In the single-block reverse runs the gap narrowed, and rsync was slightly faster on mixed-bimodal.
insights.evidence: Forward rsync-z ratios: real-congress 0.28 to 0.32, small-flat 0.36 to 0.43, mixed-bimodal 0.63 to 0.73 (3 blocks per run). Reverse: mixed-bimodal 1.04, real-congress 0.74, small-flat 0.83 (1 block each). Reverse xs-z real-congress took 12.47 s vs about 7.8 to 9.4 s forward.
insights.caveat: Reverse cells have one block each. Hypothesis only: the asymmetry may come from host CPU or storage differences between freya and neo.

insights.title: No-change re-sync: tuned setting helps real and deep trees, slightly hurts flat ones
insights.finding: Observation: on no-op copies, the tuned arm sped up small-real, real-congress and small-deep, but was slower on small-flat, where plain xs already finishes in about 0.24 s.
insights.evidence: 8 matched blocks each: small-real 1.63x (0.86 s vs 1.45 s), real-congress 1.28x, small-deep 1.27x, small-flat 0.91x. Reverse small-flat 0.97x (4 blocks). Reverse real-congress 0.97x (1 block). rsync ran 0.20 to 0.88x of plain xs.
insights.caveat: Hypothesis: small-flat may sit at a fixed startup floor where extra workers add overhead. Gains on very short runs are sensitive to timing noise.

insights.title: Incremental backups: scanning dominates real-congress, transfer dominates mixed-bimodal
insights.finding: Observation: on real-congress, xs-z time barely changes from 0.1% to 1% changed files and roughly doubles at 10%. On mixed-bimodal, time rises steadily with the changed fraction. Hypothesis: the many-file tree is limited by scanning, and the large-file tree by moving changed data.
insights.evidence: xs-z neo to freya: real-congress 1.15 s, 1.09 s, 1.98 s; mixed-bimodal 0.20 s, 0.32 s, 0.66 s (2 blocks each). Real-congress at 0.1% is close to the 1.15 s no-op time measured separately.
insights.caveat: The run was stopped. Cells have 1 to 2 blocks. The no-op comparison crosses experiments.

insights.title: Whole-file mode hurts large-file incrementals; rsync wins one 10% cell
insights.finding: Observation: whole-file xs matched xs-z on real-congress in most cells but was clearly slower on mixed-bimodal, especially at 10% changed. Separately, rsync -z beat xs-z on mixed-bimodal at 10% from neo to freya, while xs-z was far ahead on real-congress.
insights.evidence: xs-z-whole on mixed-bimodal at 10%: 0.52x (1.28 s vs 0.66 s) and 0.71x in reverse. At 1%: 0.84 to 0.89x. Real-congress: 0.97 to 1.02x, except 0.78x at 1% forward. rsync-z mixed-bimodal at 10%: 1.12x forward, 0.84x reverse. rsync-z on real-congress: 0.19 to 0.48x.
insights.caveat: Only 1 to 2 blocks per cell. Hypothesis: reusing unchanged parts of big files matters there. Sender CPU for xs-z on real-congress reverse was high (7.7 to 9.0 s vs 0.85 to 1.3 s for rsync).

insights.title: Large Mac and mars tree: xs is much faster, compression helps one way only
insights.finding: Observation: xs beat rsync in both directions on the 21 GB, 711k-file tree. Compression helped xs from Mac to mars but not from mars to Mac. Compression slowed rsync in both directions.
insights.evidence: Mac to mars (6 blocks): xs-z 3.62x (60 s vs 223 s), xs 2.73x, rsync-z 0.92x. Mars to Mac (5 blocks): xs-z 1.45x, xs 1.41x (256 s vs 272 s for xs-z), rsync-z 0.97x. Mars to Mac uses the receiver as client and shows about 600 s of client CPU.
insights.caveat: The run is still in progress. Direction is confounded with client side. The link label says 2.5 gigabit while the hypothesis mentions 10 gigabit Ethernet. The primary metric is wall time.

insights.title: Compression on incompressible data costs no time at roughly 0.93 Gb/s
insights.finding: Observation: neither adaptive compression nor level 1 changed transfer time on the large incompressible tree. Level 1 used slightly more client CPU, which contradicts the hypothesis that it would be cheaper.
insights.evidence: 8 blocks: xs 77.25 s, xs-z 0.99999x, level 1 0.99995x, all about 0.93 Gb/s. Client CPU was 51.6, 51.9 and 54.1 s.
insights.caveat: The flat throughput suggests a link ceiling. This is a hypothesis; the cost may appear on faster links.

insights.title: Sentinel self-consistency holds; smoke test ran cleanly
insights.finding: Observation: repeat-of-self ratios stayed within 3% of 1. xs vs rsync without compression was close on fresh mixed-bimodal, where rsync was slightly ahead. The incremental smoke test recorded no invalid samples in either direction.
insights.evidence: A/A ratios: 1.023, 1.001, 1.005, 1.016 (3 blocks each). rsync vs xs: fresh small-flat 0.85, fresh mixed-bimodal 1.04, no-op 0.36 and 0.68. Smoke test: 6 samples, 0 invalid, all about 0.17 to 0.21 s on a 19-byte file.
insights.caveat: No baseline values were supplied, so drift versus baseline cannot be judged. The sentinel used an older revision. The smoke data show validity, not restore correctness details.

limitations: Medians from 1 to 8 matched blocks; no confidence intervals or significance tests.
The tuned arm bundles 4 receiver workers with non-atomic writes, so the two effects are confounded.
Reverse-direction cells are mostly single blocks; direction is confounded with host hardware and, for the Mac and mars runs, with which side acts as client.
The incremental map run was stopped and the Mac and mars run is still running.
Experiments differ in revision, primary metric (durable vs wall time) and link, so cross-experiment comparisons are not controlled.
Throughput is corpus bytes divided by time, not wire rate.

Repeat the reverse direction (freya to neo) with at least 3 blocks per cell to confirm the asymmetry.
Finish the incremental map with more blocks, focusing on mixed-bimodal at 10% to test whether rsync's lead and the whole-file penalty hold.
Profile sender CPU for xs-z incrementals on real-congress from freya.
Complete the Mac and mars run and add an arm that swaps the client side.
Rerun the compression-cost test on a faster link to see whether a CPU-bound cost appears.

reports.overview: These experiments provided useful tuning insights. Here are the insights: on gigabit links, large and mixed copies already run at the wire limit, so tuning cannot add speed there. Fast compression roughly doubled delivery of text-like data from the Pi. The heaviest compression level was far slower. On the 10 gigabit link, large files reached about 9 Gb/s with default settings, and extra streams, workers or queues did not help. The best small-file setting helped small trees and did not slow mixed or large trees, but this is still provisional. Pulling small trees onto the Mac is much slower than pushing them. Several runs were small, stopped, failed or running, so most gains need confirmation.

insights.title: Fast compression doubles gigabit delivery of text; the heavy level collapses
insights.finding: On large text sent from the Pi over gigabit, xs with compression and xs at level 1 delivered about twice the link rate. Level 3 and rsync with compression were much slower than uncompressed xs.
insights.evidence: Speed vs plain xs, 2 matched blocks each: xs-z 2.10x (1.95 Gb/s), xs-z1 2.04x, rsync-z 0.63x, xs-z3 0.36x (0.33 Gb/s). Client CPU: 52 s plain, 124 s xs-z, 726 s xs-z3.
insights.caveat: There are only two blocks, on one compressible corpus. A hypothesis is that level 3 saturates the Pi CPU; CPU time is consistent with this but does not prove it.

insights.title: Gigabit wire is the ceiling for large and mixed trees
insights.finding: Large text ran at about 0.93 Gb/s for xs and rsync in every gigabit cell. On mixed-bimodal from the Pi, rsync was slightly faster while using less than half the client CPU.
insights.evidence: Large text: NE1 xs 0.930 vs rsync 0.930 Gb/s (6 blocks); H6 0.926 to 0.931 Gb/s (8 blocks). Mixed-bimodal neo to freya, rsync vs xs: 1.048x (NE1, 6 blocks), 1.039x (D9, 8 blocks), 1.013x (S0, 3 blocks). CPU was about 5.0 s for rsync vs 11.6 to 12.2 s for xs.
insights.caveat: Reverse-direction cells have only 1 to 2 blocks. The small rsync edge is a median, not a significance result.

insights.title: Small trees: xs about twice rsync, best setting adds more without hurting mixed or large trees
insights.finding: xs consistently beat rsync on 100k-file trees. The xs-best arm (4 receiver workers, no atomic writes) helped further on small trees and stayed neutral on mixed and large trees.
insights.evidence: rsync vs xs on small trees: 0.47x (D9 small-opaque, 8 blocks), 0.48x (S0 small-flat, 3 blocks), 0.63x (G2 ZFS small-flat, 8 blocks). xs-best vs xs: 1.13x (D9, 8 blocks), 1.44x on ZFS (8 blocks), 1.65x and 1.80x (G0, 1 block each). On mixed and large trees H6 ranged 0.993 to 1.006x (8 blocks) and D9 0.993 to 1.018x.
insights.caveat: xs-best gives up atomic writes, which is a durability tradeoff. The G0 cells are single samples.

insights.title: 10GbE large files near line rate by default; extra parallelism hurts mixed trees
insights.finding: Default xs moved large text at about 9.2 Gb/s pushing and 8.8 Gb/s pulling. None of the stream, block, queue or worker variants helped large files, and higher parallelism slowed mixed trees.
insights.evidence: G1 (8 blocks per cell): on large text, every variant fell between 0.967x and 1.003x. On mixed-bimodal mac to freya, jobs16 was 0.91x, all-four 0.90x and streams8 0.95x, while block4m was 1.01x. Pulling, every variant fell between 0.95x and 0.98x. G0: rsync 0.49x and 0.43x on large text (1 block each).
insights.caveat: This held on one host pair. Pull mixed throughput (3.0 Gb/s) was far below push (7.1 Gb/s), a direction effect these variants did not address.

insights.title: ZFS pool lands large files at about 7 Gb/s; larger writes are mixed
insights.finding: Landing on the raidz2 pool, xs reached about 6.9 Gb/s for large text, roughly double rsync. The write1m arm was neutral on large files but slower on mixed trees.
insights.evidence: G2 (8 blocks each): large text xs 6.94 Gb/s, rsync 0.52x, write1m 1.018x, xs-best 1.008x. Mixed-bimodal: write1m 0.92x, rsync 0.51x. Small-flat: xs-best 1.44x, write1m 1.02x.
insights.caveat: 48 of 144 samples were invalid, so the valid set may be biased. About 7 Gb/s is below the hypothesized close to 10 Gb/s.

insights.title: Batching and scanning variants: direction-dependent, within noise or regressions
insights.finding: In the failed 10GbE small-tree run, scan-all and all-three helped mixed trees pulled to the Mac. The same variants regressed on many-file real trees in that direction. Level 1 compression was the only arm never clearly slower.
insights.evidence: G3 (2 blocks): mixed-bimodal pull scan-all 1.16x, all-three 1.15x, z1-best 1.11x. Real-congress pull all-three 0.90x, coalesce1m 0.89x, z1-best 1.04x. Mixed-bimodal push z1-best 1.11x. Pulls were much slower than pushes: small-deep 40.3 s vs 6.4 s, real-congress 32.5 s vs 6.9 s.
insights.caveat: The run failed and has 2 or fewer blocks per cell. Treat these results as screening signals only. Why pulls are slow is an open question; Mac receive-side file creation is a hypothesis.

insights.title: Pi as receiver is the small-file ceiling; compression and 4 workers matter for Pi transfers
insights.finding: Local file creation on the Pi was no faster than xs delivery, which points to the Pi itself as the limit. Local creation on mars was much faster, so mars is not the limit when the Pi sends. Fewer receive workers and turning compression off both slowed real trees.
insights.evidence: H1a, Pi local with 4 streams vs xs: 0.63x real-congress, 1.00x small-deep, 0.81x small-flat (4 to 5 blocks). H1b, mars local with 4 streams: 3.84x to 4.53x (8 blocks). H4: recv1 0.83x real-congress and 0.76x small-deep; recv2 0.94x to 1.02x; xs-best without compression 0.83x (1 block). D3: xs-best without compression 0.81x and send3 0.83x on real-congress (2 to 3 blocks); batch256 and coalesce1m were within 1.3% of the control.
insights.caveat: Many cells have 1 to 3 blocks, and D3 was stopped. The compression benefit on real-congress is an observation, not yet explained.

insights.title: No-op speed and drift checks; one run produced no data
insights.finding: xs was faster than rsync on warm no-op copies, contradicting the Mac push hypothesis. Same-tool repeat checks mostly stayed within 3%. The bidirectional Mac and mars run had only invalid samples.
insights.evidence: MA1: xs 6.93x rsync (1 block). S0 rsync vs xs: 0.38x small-flat no-op and 0.68x mixed no-op (3 blocks). Repeat arm: 0.99x to 1.00x on fresh copies, 0.94x mixed no-op (3 blocks), 1.06x reverse (1 block). MA3: 4 of 4 samples invalid.
insights.caveat: No-op times are 0.2 to 0.3 s, so small absolute jitter produces large ratios. MA1 has a single sample and was stopped.

limitations: Medians of matched-block ratios only; no confidence intervals or significance tests.
Many cells have 1 to 3 blocks, especially reverse directions, G0, H4 and G3.
G3 failed, D3 and MA1 were stopped, MA3 is running with all samples invalid, and G2 had 48 of 144 samples invalid.
Runs differ in hosts, links, revisions and controls, so cross-run comparisons are not controlled.
xs-best variants disable atomic writes, which confounds speed with durability semantics.
Throughput is corpus bytes divided by duration, not measured wire rate.
nextSteps: Repeat the level 1 compression vs plain xs comparison across corpora of varying compressibility, both directions, with at least 8 blocks.
Run a controlled 8-block test isolating 4 receiver workers from disabling atomic writes on small trees, including on ZFS.
Investigate slow pulls to the Mac with a local file-creation ceiling test on the Mac, like H1a and H1b.
Rerun the G3 scan-all and all-three arms on mixed and real trees pulled to the Mac with more blocks.
Fix the invalid-sample cause in MA3 and G2 before trusting those cells.

reports.overview: These experiments provided useful tuning insights. Here are the insights: On the fast link, xs moved large files at nearly full speed in both directions and beat rsync in every test. Folders with many small files stayed far below link speed, especially when copying from freya to mac. Turning off atomic writes made those copies roughly 1.5 to 2 times faster in that direction. However, it gives up a safety guarantee and did not help large files, so treat it as a provisional candidate, not a default. On the slower link, the Pi created files locally no faster than xs delivered them, so local file creation does not look like the limit there. All results rest on very few repeats.

insights.title: H1a: local creation on neo did not outpace xs delivery
insights.finding: Observation: the hypothesis that the Pi creates small files locally much faster than xs delivers them is not supported in this window. Both local arms were slower than xs-z-best on real-congress and small-flat, and roughly tied on small-deep.
insights.evidence:
Paired speed vs xs-z-best:
- real-congress: local-x1 0.31 and local-x4 0.63 (2 blocks each); medians 34.79 s and 16.83 s vs 10.81 s (3 blocks).
- small-flat: local-x1 0.39 and local-x4 0.78 (3 blocks); 9.37 s and 4.63 s vs 3.61 s.
- small-deep: local-x1 0.93 and local-x4 0.99 (3 blocks).
insights.caveat: Only 2 to 3 blocks per arm, and the run is still in progress. What the local arms measure exactly (creation path, durability semantics) is not described in the evidence, so the comparison may not be like-for-like.

insights.title: Local parallelism helps flat trees but not deep trees
insights.finding: Observation: going from local-x1 to local-x4 roughly halved duration on real-congress and small-flat. On small-deep it gave only about an 11 percent gain. Hypothesis: deep directory structure imposes a serialization cost (for example directory creation or metadata) that extra workers do not relieve.
insights.evidence:
Median durations, local-x1 to local-x4:
- real-congress: 34.79 s to 16.83 s, about 2.07x.
- small-flat: 9.37 s to 4.63 s, about 2.03x.
- small-deep: 14.36 s to 12.97 s, about 1.11x.
Client CPU rose with x4 in every case: 14.12 to 19.88 s, 4.06 to 5.59 s, and 12.31 to 15.10 s.
insights.caveat: These are cross-arm medians within a cell, not paired ratios. Real-congress has only 2 blocks per local arm.

insights.title: small-deep shows a shared ceiling of about 0.18 to 0.20 Gb/s on neo
insights.finding: Observation: small-deep has the same 100,000 files and 319 MB as small-flat. Yet xs-z-best took 13.46 s on small-deep vs 3.61 s on small-flat, and all three arms converged near 13 to 14 s. Hypothesis: a receiver-side metadata or storage bottleneck on neo for deep trees caps both local creation and network delivery.
insights.evidence:
small-deep medians:
- xs-z-best: 13.46 s, 0.19 Gb/s.
- local-x4: 12.97 s, 0.20 Gb/s.
- local-x1: 14.36 s, 0.18 Gb/s.
small-flat xs-z-best: 3.61 s, 0.71 Gb/s.
All cells have 3 blocks.
insights.caveat: The bottleneck location is inferred, not measured. No per-host CPU or I/O data are supplied.

insights.title: G0: xs reaches the large-file target in both directions
insights.finding: Observation: on large-text (8 files, 8.59 GB), xs and xs-best both exceeded 80 percent of 10GbE in both directions. This supports the first part of the G0 hypothesis. xs-best was neutral relative to xs for large files.
insights.evidence:
mac to freya:
- xs: 9.35 Gb/s (7.35 s).
- xs-best: 9.33 Gb/s, speed 0.997.
freya to mac:
- xs: 8.85 Gb/s (7.77 s).
- xs-best: 8.86 Gb/s, speed 1.001.
Each cell has 1 paired block.
insights.caveat: A single block per cell. Gb/s is corpus bytes divided by durable_s, not the wire rate.

insights.title: xs beat rsync in every G0 cell, most strongly on real-congress and large files
insights.finding: Observation: rsync was slower than xs in all 8 cells, consistent with the second part of the G0 hypothesis. The margin was largest for mac to freya real-congress and mixed-bimodal, and smallest for small-flat.

rsync paired speed vs xs:
- real-congress: 0.28 mac to freya, 0.61 freya to mac.
- mixed-bimodal: 0.34 mac to freya, 0.49 freya to mac.
- large-text: 0.47 mac to freya, 0.40 freya to mac.
- small-flat: 0.78 mac to freya, 0.63 freya to mac.
Each is 1 paired block. On large files rsync topped out at 4.44 and 3.57 Gb/s.
insights.caveat: One paired block per cell, and real-congress freya to mac has only 1 paired block despite 2 rsync samples. Consistency across cells is suggestive, not a significance result.

insights.title: Strong direction asymmetry for many-file trees on the 10G pair
insights.finding: Observation: freya to mac transfers of many-file trees were much slower than mac to freya. Large files were nearly symmetric. Hypothesis: per-file create or durability cost on mac as receiver, or the receiver-client mode, dominates. Direction, client role and destination storage are fully confounded here, so the cause cannot be isolated.
insights.evidence:
xs medians, mac to freya vs freya to mac:
- real-congress: 6.82 s vs 40.28 s (about 5.9x).
- small-flat: 3.54 s vs 16.00 s (about 4.5x).
- mixed-bimodal: 1.55 s vs 3.60 s (about 2.3x).
- large-text: 7.35 s vs 7.77 s.
Many-file ceilings stayed far below link rate. The best real-congress result was 1.43 Gb/s and the best small-flat result 1.15 Gb/s.
insights.caveat: These are cross-cell comparisons with different client roles (sender vs receiver), not a controlled direction test. Most cells have 1 block, and freya to mac real-congress xs has 1 sample.

insights.title: xs-best gains concentrate on many-file trees, especially freya to mac
insights.finding: Observation: xs-best improved substantially on xs for small-flat and real-congress in the slow freya to mac direction, and for small-flat mac to freya. It was neutral or slightly negative elsewhere. In freya to mac it also used less client CPU. Hypothesis: the tuned settings relieve per-file overhead rather than bulk bandwidth.
insights.evidence:
freya to mac, xs-best vs xs:
- small-flat: 2.05x faster; CPU 9.33 vs 17.21 s.
- mixed-bimodal: 1.59x; CPU 3.84 vs 5.13 s.
- real-congress: 1.54x (1 paired block); CPU 50.03 vs 61.25 s.
mac to freya, xs-best vs xs:
- small-flat: 1.59x; CPU 14.33 vs 13.67 s.
- real-congress: 1.05x.
- mixed-bimodal: 0.97x.
- large-text: 0.997x.
insights.caveat: The settings behind xs-best are not specified in the evidence. Each ratio rests on a single paired block, so the 0.97 and 1.05 values are indistinguishable from parity at this sample size.

insights.title: CPU tradeoffs: xs spends more mac CPU than rsync when mac sends, less when mac receives
insights.finding: Observation: mac is the client in both G0 directions. When mac sends small-flat, xs used about 2.9x rsync's client CPU for a 1.28x speedup. When mac receives, xs used less CPU than rsync while also being faster. In H1a, xs-z-best used less sender CPU than local-x4 on flat trees.
insights.evidence:
G0 client CPU on mac:
- small-flat mac to freya: xs 13.67 s vs rsync 4.66 s.
- real-congress mac to freya: xs 32.96 s vs rsync 23.13 s.
- small-flat freya to mac: xs 17.21 s vs rsync 25.98 s.
- real-congress freya to mac: xs 61.25 s vs rsync 84.17 s.
H1a client CPU, xs-z-best vs local-x4:
- small-flat: 2.37 s vs 5.59 s.
- real-congress: 12.57 s vs 19.88 s.
insights.caveat: Only client-side CPU is reported, not remote-side CPU. In H1a, what client CPU means for the local arms is unclear. The G0 figures are single-block medians.

limitations: Both runs are still running. G0 cells mostly have 1 block, and H1a cells have 2 to 3 blocks.
The supplied values are medians and matched-block ratios, with no confidence intervals or significance tests.
Real-congress freya to mac in G0 has only 1 paired block, and its xs control has 1 sample.
In G0, direction, client role (sender vs receiver) and destination storage are confounded.
The H1a and G0 runs use different hosts, links and arms, so cross-run comparisons are not controlled.
Arm configurations (xs-best, xs-z-best, local-x1, local-x4) are not detailed. Interactions with worker, stream or compression settings therefore cannot be attributed.
Only client CPU is reported. There is no remote CPU, disk or network telemetry to locate bottlenecks.
All cells are fresh scenario with a warm cache. Cold-cache and incremental behavior are untested here.
nextSteps: Let both runs accumulate at least 3 to 5 paired blocks per cell before drawing conclusions, especially in G0.
Revisit or reword the H1a hypothesis given that local creation was slower than xs-z-best on flat trees.
Investigate the small-deep plateau on neo with receiver-side CPU and I/O tracing, and with higher local worker counts.
Separate direction from client role in G0. Run freya to mac with a sender-side client, and mac to freya with a receiver-side client.
Ablate the individual settings in xs-best to see which one drives the 1.5x to 2x many-file gains in freya to mac.
Collect remote-side CPU to judge the xs vs rsync CPU tradeoff fully.

tuningImplications.recommendation: Keep xs-z-best as the comparison baseline for this pair. The hypothesis that the Pi creates small files locally much faster than xs delivers them from mars is not supported so far. Local creation was slower than xs on real-congress (local-x1 0.31, local-x4 0.63 paired speed) and small-flat (0.39, 0.78). On small-deep all three arms were close at about 13 to 14 s (0.93, 0.99). Local creation does not appear to be the ceiling on these corpora, though small-deep may be bound by the same cost for every arm. The run is still in progress, so this is screening evidence only.
tuningImplications.tradeoffs: local-x4 used more client CPU than xs-z-best on real-congress (19.9 vs 12.6 s) and small-flat (5.6 vs 2.4 s). The control runs with --no-atomic, so it is not a durability-equivalent baseline. Any atomic-mode ceiling remains unmeasured. Scope is limited to mars to neo, the 1g link, warm cache, fresh scenario and sender client.
tuningImplications.evidenceStrength: Weak: run still running, 2 to 3 paired blocks per cell, medians only.
tuningImplications.nextTest: Finish the run with at least 5 blocks per cell. Add an atomic xs arm to separate the durability cost. Repeat small-deep with cold cache to check whether all arms share a filesystem limit.

tuningImplications.recommendation: For large files, the hypothesis is supported on single blocks. Default xs reached about 8.85 Gbps (freya to mac) and 9.35 Gbps (mac to freya), both above 80% of 10GbE. xs was faster than rsync on every tree, at 0.28 to 0.78 paired speed for rsync. Treat xs-best (--no-atomic) as a candidate only for many-file trees, mainly in the freya to mac receiver-client direction: 2.05 on small-flat, 1.60 on mixed-bimodal and 1.44 on real-congress. In the mac to freya direction it gained only on small-flat (1.59, 1 block) and was neutral on mixed-bimodal and real-congress (0.99, 1.05). It is neutral on large-text, so there is no reason to use it there. Do not adopt it as a default on this evidence.
tuningImplications.tradeoffs: --no-atomic gives up atomic writes, and that durability cost was not measured here. xs-best also lowered client CPU in freya to mac (small-flat 9.3 vs 17.2 s, real-congress 50.0 vs 59.5 s). rsync used much less client CPU than xs on mac to freya small-flat (4.7 vs 13.7 s), but it was slower.
tuningImplications.evidenceStrength: Weak to moderate: run complete, but most cells have 1 block and the rest have 2. Results are warm-cache, fresh-scenario medians only.
tuningImplications.nextTest: Repeat with 5 or more blocks per direction for xs vs xs-best on small-flat, mixed-bimodal and real-congress. Add crash or fsync durability checks for --no-atomic and test with cold cache.
